new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable; further (secondary) stresses on every second syllable to the left of it (right-to-left trochaic alternation). Stated tentatively ('seems to').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating: every other syllable counting leftward from the penult (implied by 'alternate syllables counting backwards'); Heineman 1998's transcription [ˌma.ⁿdi.ˈli.me] 'she is carrying' shows exactly this.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The statement is hedged ('seems to'); no lexical exceptions, no weight sensitivity, no tone reported.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a 3-page SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet based on citation forms; final vowels are 'generally devoiced, and sometimes dropped completely' (same page), which can make penult stress surface as final in fast speech, but the source does not discuss this interaction. Heineman's 1998 grammar (106 pp., same author) states no stress rule but its stress-marked phonetic forms all agree with penult + alternating secondary.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Lembena [leq] = lemb1266 itself (OPD locates it at Yankisa and neighbouring villages, East Sepik/Enga border; grammar data from Itopeno village and others, 1991-1996). No dialect split is described. The OPD was catalogued by SIL as 'Anonymous, n.d.' but its own bibliography attributes the data to Paul and Marcia Heineman (1994).

sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology (pp. 8-9) gives phoneme inventory, six allophonic conventions, syllable patterns (V, VV, CV, CVV) and ordered morphophonemic rules; no stress/accent/tone statement anywhere in the text (grep of full text: zero hits for stress/accent/tone/pitch). Phonetic examples carry stress marks that are all consistent with penult primary + alternating secondary: [ˈa.ɾa] 'sit', [a.ˈⁿda.qa] 'at the house', [ˈa.ⁿda] 'house', [ˌma.ⁿdi.ˈli.me] 'she is carrying', [a.ˈpe.ɺe] 'rain'.
